facts.claim: The song was written by Lucius members Holly Laessig and Jess Wolfe together with Trent Dabbs.
The Piano Version single came out on 6 October 2022 on Mom+Pop. It has two tracks, the piano version and the original album version.

Wolfe says the writing trip to Nashville was in early March 2020 to do preliminary writing for an upcoming record. The trio wrote the song at Sheryl Crow's piano in her living room, and Crow was the first person to hear them play it.
Wolfe says the piano version was meant to feel like that first listen: honest, pure and on the edge of a very vulnerable time.
Laessig described the song as exploring the idea of finding love again and opening yourself back up to the possibility.
Consequence reports that the song addresses the end of Wolfe's marriage to Lucius drummer Dan Molad.
The original version is on the album Second Nature, released April 8, 2022. Dave Cobb and Brandi Carlile produced the album.
Pitchfork called the song home to one of the album's best choruses.
Lucius played the song on The Kelly Clarkson Show. They performed it at KEXP with a band of Dan Molad, Peter Lalish, Solomon Dorsey and Alex Pfender.
Lucius is an American indie pop band from Brooklyn, New York, formed in 2011. It is led by vocalists Jess Wolfe and Holly Laessig.

research.lineage: The song sits in Lucius's harmony-driven indie pop, and the piano version strips it back toward the Nashville-songwriter setting where it was written.

draft:
Two voices sing as one over a piano that keeps rolling its chords upward, each note held under the next. In this stripped-down **The Man I'll Never Find**, the unison is the whole drama. The voices are breathy and sustained, so tightly blended that it's hard to hear where one ends and the other begins. The piano holds a gentle, flowing arpeggio at a slow tempo, and it never pushes. The room is medium-sized and lightly reverberant, and the production is clean. Nothing else gets in the way.

The song began in a living room. In early March 2020, Lucius's Jess Wolfe and Holly Laessig went to Nashville with songwriter Trent Dabbs to start writing for a new record. They wrote this one at Sheryl Crow's piano, and Crow was the first person to hear it. Wolfe says the piano version was meant to recreate that first listen: honest, pure, and "on the edge of a very vulnerable time." That explains the restraint. This version doesn't take apart a finished production so much as return to the moment before there was one.

What it carries is two feelings that don't settle. Consequence reports that the song addresses the end of Wolfe's marriage to Lucius drummer Dan Molad. Laessig describes it as being about finding love again and opening yourself back up to the possibility. The title points the other way, toward a search already given up on. Grief and hope sit in the same song, and the piano version gives neither the last word. Two voices singing the same line fit that tension. They sound like one person talking herself through something, with a friend saying every word alongside her.

There's another layer outside the recording. When Lucius played the song at KEXP, the backing band included Molad on drums, along with Peter Lalish, Solomon Dorsey, and Alex Pfender. A song about the end of a marriage, played with the other half of that marriage in the room, says a lot about how complicated an ending can be.

The original appears on *Second Nature*, which Dave Cobb and Brandi Carlile produced, and Pitchfork singled out its chorus as one of the album's best. The album version belongs to Lucius's polished, harmony-driven indie pop. This one leans toward the Nashville writing room, where a song has to work with just a piano and a voice or two. It holds up. The melody doesn't need the arrangement to sound big.

The two voices moving as one make heartbreak sound like something you don't have to carry alone, even while the song admits the loss is real.
